title: Most Frequent Piece Under a Letter Limit
statement:
You get a lowercase string s and three numbers maxLetters, minSize and maxSize. A substring of s is allowed if its length is between minSize and maxSize (inclusive) and it uses at most maxLetters different letters.

Return the largest number of times any one allowed substring occurs in s. Occurrences may overlap. Return 0 if no substring is allowed.

examples.why: "ab" starts at 0, 3 and 6. Every allowed length-3 piece, like "abc", appears only twice.
"aa" starts at 0, 1 and 2. Overlapping occurrences count.
Every length-3 piece has 3 different letters, so none is allowed.

constraints: s has only lowercase English letters
hints: Suppose some longer allowed piece occurs t times. What can you say about its first minSize letters?
The prefix of length minSize occurs at least t times too, and it uses no more letters than the longer piece. So maxSize never matters.
Slide a window of exactly minSize over s, keep letter counts to know how many distinct letters are inside, and count each allowed window in a hash map.

explain.intuition:
The trick is that longer pieces never win. If a piece of length L > minSize occurs t times, its first minSize letters occur at each of those same starting points, so at least t times. And a prefix has at most as many different letters as the whole piece, so it is allowed too. That means you only need to look at windows of length exactly minSize, and maxSize can be ignored.

Then it is a fixed-size sliding window: maintain counts of the letters inside and the number of distinct letters, and every time the window is allowed, bump that substring's count in a hash map.
steps: Keep count[26] for the letters in the window, distinct, and a map seen from substring to occurrences.
Move the right end over s. Add the new letter; if its count became 1, increase distinct.
If the window is longer than minSize, remove the leftmost letter; if its count became 0, decrease distinct.
When the window has length minSize and distinct ≤ maxLetters, increase seen for that substring and update the best.
Return the best count (0 if nothing was allowed).
pitfalls: Counting only non-overlapping occurrences. In "aaaa", "aa" occurs 3 times.
Trying every length from minSize to maxSize. It gives the same answer but costs up to 26 times more work.
Counting distinct letters in each window from scratch with a set; it works but is slower. The running distinct counter is what makes the window cheap.

complexity.time: O(n × minSize) for building window strings (O(n) with rolling hashes)

solutions.title: Every length from minSize to maxSize
solutions.idea: For each allowed length and each start, take the substring, check its distinct letters, and count it.

solutions.title: Sliding window of exactly minSize
solutions.idea: Any longer allowed piece has an allowed minSize prefix that occurs at least as often, so only windows of length minSize matter.

followups: minSize can be up to 100 000. How do rolling hashes keep the window O(1) per step, and how do you handle collisions?
Return the substring itself, choosing the lexicographically smallest on ties.
lcTitle: Maximum Number of Occurrences of a Substring
